title: Ketogenic diet as a therapeutic intervention for biochemical hyperandrogenism in PCOS women with obesity or overweight: a meta-analytic study
abstract: PurposeTo assess whether the Ketogenic Diet (KD) is associated with improvements in biochemical markers of hyperandrogenism in women diagnosed with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) with obesity or overweight.MethodsA systematic search was conducted in five databases: MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Scopus, and Web of Science. Both RCTs and pre-post studies providing data for direct extraction or calculation of mean (SD) changes in the investigated outcomes, published until March 1, 2025, were considered. Protocols included “Very Low” and “Low” Calories KD, and modified KD regimens. The primary outcome was the effect of the KD on total testosterone (TT), Free T (FT) and Sex Hormone Binding Globulin (SHBG) compared to baseline.ResultsThe KD was found to be associated with a statistically significant reduction in TT (n = 290, Mean Difference [MD] -0.35, CI -0.46; -0.24) and a significant increase in SHBG levels (n = 144, MD 19.50, CI 6.90; 32.11), independently of study design. When considering only RCTs (4 studies), the KD showed a moderate, statistically significant benefit on TT levels compared to the control intervention, with a high heterogeneity (n = 115 vs. 117, SMD -0.284, CI -0.543, -0.035; p = 0.031). Neither the duration of the KD protocol, the change in BMI, the change in fasting insulin levels nor the change in LH/FSH ratio were able to significantly affect the change in TT levels observed over time. In addition, the KD associated with a significant reduction in LH levels (n = 275, MD -3.48, CI -4.71; -2.26) and in the LH/FSH ratio (n = 275, MD -0.99, CI -1.44; -0.54).ConclusionOur meta-analysis indicates a reduced biochemical hyperandrogenism—particularly a reduction in TT—and a reduction in the LH/FSH ratio among women with PCOS following a KD. Our findings also suggest a specific effect of ketosis on ovarian function acting alongside metabolic improvements, but a direct causal link cannot be definitively established. Owing to the low quality and heterogeneous nature of the available studies, larger, high-quality RCTs are essential to consolidate this evidence and determine clinical efficacy.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40618-026-02924-1.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is one of the most common endocrine disorders affecting women of reproductive age, with a prevalence of 10–13% []. The underlying pathogenic mechanisms and risk factors for PCOS are complex and not yet fully understood, with a highly heterogeneous presentation and a significant long-term risk for cardiovascular morbidity []. However, research consistently highlights the significant role of metabolic features in the clinical characteristics and complications of the syndrome. As a result, lifestyle intervention is currently regarded as a first line therapy for PCOS. Specifically, exercise alone, or a combination of diet, exercise, and behavioral strategies, is recommended for all women with PCOS to improve metabolic health, including reducing central adiposity and improving lipid profiles [, ]. Weight loss interventions are of particular importance in PCOS women with overweight and obesity, since it is recognized that many patients tend to obtain a greater longitudinal weight gain, and/or face greater challenges with weight management compared to non-PCOS women [].

Although no conclusive evidence supports the superiority of any one diet over another in terms of anthropometric, metabolic, hormonal, reproductive, or psychological outcomes [], growing research suggests that calorie-restricted diets and low-energy, low-carbohydrate combination diets may offer advantages over other dietary interventions, particularly in improving clinical manifestations and pregnancy rates in individuals with PCOS and a body mass index (BMI) ≥ 25 kg/m2 [].

Among dietary protocols characterized by low carbohydrate intake, the Ketogenic Diet (KD) is distinguished by its high fat content (> 70% of total caloric intake) while limiting excess protein consumption []. This approach promotes the production of ketone bodies—primarily acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate—leading to a state of nutritional ketosis. A specific variation of KD, the very low-calorie ketogenic diet (VLCKD), involves a daily carbohydrate intake of less than 30 g/day (approximately 13% of total energy intake), with relatively higher proportions of fat (~ 44%) and protein (~ 43%), while maintaining a total daily energy intake of less than 800 kcal []. Recently, VLCKD has been redefined as Very Low-Energy Ketogenic Therapy (VLEKT) by a panel of Italian experts [], and it has been proposed as a therapeutic approach for obesity. In 2019, the Italian Society of Endocrinology (SIE) recognized PCOS-associated obesity as one of its indications, albeit with a weak recommendation due to the limited evidence available at the time []. Since then, evidence has been accumulating; however, no updated consensus has been issued to strengthen the recommendation.

In this context, studying the effects of nutritional ketosis on hormonal and reproductive parameters—key aspects of PCOS clinical presentation—is particularly important. This research is essential for providing healthcare providers with updated evidence-based data to guide nutritional strategies for PCOS patients in relation to the desired outcomes. A preliminary meta-analysis published in 2023 by Khalid et al. [] summarized data from 7 studies, indicating improvements in androgen profiles. However, since then, new trials have been published, and a more detailed exploration of the mechanisms—specifically the interplay between metabolic changes and hormonal shifts—is warranted.

sections.title: Aim
sections.text:
The primary objective of this meta-analysis is to assess whether the KD—in the form of VLCKD, LCKD, or modified KD —is associated with improvements in biochemical markers of hyperandrogenism in PCOS women with obesity or overweight. According to International Guidelines [], most studies use total (TT) and free testosterone (FT) to assess biochemical hyperandrogenism in the diagnosis of PCOS; therefore, the primary outcomes of the present study were changes in TT and FT, independently of the method of measurement.

Secondarily, we explored whether KD protocols are associated with a change in luteinizing hormone/follicle stimulating hormone (LH/FSH) ratio. It is believed that PCOS women show a powerful LH secretion by the anterior pituitary due to a constitutional increase in the frequency and amplitude of gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) pulses []. PCOS patients also exhibit decreased FSH levels, leading to an increased LH/FSH ratio, which in turn stimulates excess androgen production from ovarian theca cells and ultimately disrupts follicular development and ovulation []. For many years, an elevated LH/FSH ratio was used as a diagnostic marker for PCOS []. However, it is no longer recommended due to its limited clinical utility []. Nevertheless, it has been linked to TT levels [] and proposed as a predictor of poor outcomes in Medically Assisted Reproduction []. Finally, the effectiveness of the KD in reducing body weight and visceral fat, as well as improving body composition and the glyco-lipid profile, was evaluated.

All available studies were considered, including randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and non-randomized prospective or retrospective observational studies. The outcomes analyzed include TT, Sex Hormones Binding Globulin (SHBG), FT, LH, FSH, the LH/FSH ratio, BMI, waist circumference (WC), fat mass, fasting glucose, fasting insulin, Homeostatic Model Assessment (HOMA)-insulin resistance (IR) index, total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and triglycerides levels.

An initial objective was to evaluate the effects of the KD on menstrual cycle regularity and reproductive outcomes; however, due to heterogeneity in study variables and methodology, a meta-analysis of these outcomes was not feasible.

sections.title: Methods
sections.text:
This research was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42023389506).

A systematic search was conducted in five databases: MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Scopus, and Web of Science. No language restrictions were applied. The URL for the search strategy was: ("diet, ketogenic"[MeSH Terms] OR ("diet"[All Fields] AND "ketogenic"[All Fields]) OR "ketogenic diet"[All Fields] OR ("ketogenic"[All Fields] AND "diet"[All Fields])) AND "PCOS"[All Fields] AND ("VLCKD"[All Fields] AND ("ketogenic"[All Fields] AND ("polycystic ovary syndrome"[MeSH Terms] OR ("polycystic"[All Fields] AND "ovary"[All Fields] AND "syndrome"[All Fields]) OR "polycystic ovary syndrome"[All Fields])) AND ("VLCKD"[All Fields] AND ("polycystic ovary syndrome"[MeSH Terms] OR ("polycystic"[All Fields] AND "ovary"[All Fields] AND "syndrome"[All Fields]) OR "polycystic ovary syndrome" [All Fields])).

All studies published until March 1, 2025, were considered.

Both RCTs and pre-post studies providing data for direct extraction or calculation of mean (SD) changes in the considered outcomes were included.

Inclusion criteria for participants were a diagnosis of PCOS based on the Rotterdam or European Society for Human Reproduction and Embryology/American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ESHRE/ASRM) criteria [], aged 18 years or older, within reproductive age, and with a BMI of at least 25 kg/m2. Exclusion criteria were pregnancy and serious medical conditions requiring medical supervision.

Eligible studies involved participants treated with a KD, including VLCKD protocols (approximately 800 kcal/day) and LCKD protocols (1200–1400 kcal/day). Both protocols were characterized by low carbohydrate intake (≤ 50 g/day), 1–1.5 g of protein per kilogram of ideal body weight, and fat intake of less than 20–30 g/day. Modified KD regimens were also included.

Studies involving medical infertility treatments were included only if the data were collected during the dietary protocols and prior to the initiation of any medical treatment.

The primary outcome of this meta-analysis was the effect of the KD on TT, FT and SHBG levels compared to baseline. TT levels were included when measured using both the gold-standard method, tandem mass spectrometry (LC/MS), and immunologic assays. FT in the included studies was assessed by direct immunoassays. Additional hormonal outcomes included the KD’s impact on LH, FSH, and the LH/FSH ratio compared to baseline.

Although follow-up data were initially planned to include two observation periods (3 and 6 months), the studies analyzed had inconsistent or unique follow-up timelines; therefore, data closest to the 6-month follow-up were selected.

The effect measure was expressed as the mean difference (MD).

Secondary outcomes included BMI, WC, WHR, fat mass, fasting glucose, fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol and LDL cholesterol. Reproductive outcomes considered were menstrual cycle regularization, ovulation, and pregnancy achievement. However, due to variability in evaluation methods, these outcomes were assessed qualitatively rather than quantitatively.

Unpublished studies were identified through a search on ClinicalTrials.gov. Two researchers (EM and CA) independently conducted the identification of relevant abstracts, study selection, and data extraction from full-text articles. Extracted information included the author, year of publication, study design, diagnostic criteria, study population (sample size), number of participants in the intention-to-treat analysis, mean age and age range, inclusion and exclusion criteria, duration of dietary intervention (in days), type of KD, and outcome indicators (mean and standard deviation or SEM; success rate for categorical variables). If articles lacked sufficient information, the authors were contacted for additional data. Discrepancies between the two investigators were resolved discussion with a third author (GV).

Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using the I2 statistic, which quantifies the percentage of variation across studies. Since heterogeneity was significant, a random-effects model was applied to calculate the effect size, assuming that different studies estimated related but distinct interventions. All analyses were performed using StataCorp software, version 18 (Stata Statistical Software: Release 18. College Station, TX: StataCorp LLC).

The quality of included studies was evaluated using the following tools: Cochrane’s Risk of Bias Tool for Non-Randomized Studies (ROBINS-I) [] for RCTs;NIH Quality Assessment Tool for Before-After (Pre-Post) Studies With No Control Group [] for pre-post studies.

For all meta-analyses, significant heterogeneity among studies was observed; therefore, a random-effects model was used for effect size calculation.

Sensitivity analyses were conducted according to the study design (RCTs, prospective and retrospective) for all outcomes, and are reported in each Figure. For RCTs, “before” and “after” data regarding the KD arm of study were considered.

The KD was found to be associated with a statistically significant reduction in TT (n = 290, MD -0.35, CI -0.46; -0.24) (Fig. 2) and a significant increase in SHBG levels (n = 144, MD 19.50, CI 6.90; 32.11) (Fig. 3), independently of study design. For each of the tested outcomes, a sensitivity analysis using the "leave-one-out" principle revealed that the overall effect estimate did not significantly change when each study was excluded (not shown). In order to investigate the factors possibly affecting the change in TT levels, we next performed meta-regression analyses. Although these meta-regressions can be limited by the small number of studies, neither the duration of the KD protocol, the change in BMI, the change in fasting insulin levels nor the change in LH/FSH ratio, were able to significantly affect the change in TT levels observed over time. Similarly, neither the change in fasting insulin levels nor the change in BMI affected the decrease in FT levels (not shown).

In addition, the KD associated with a significant reduction in LH levels (n = 275, MD -3.48, CI -4.71; -2.26) (Fig. 5) and, even though it did not reach a statistical significance, an increase in FSH levels was also observed (n = 275, MD 0.52, CI -0.30; 1.34) (Fig. 6). Therefore, the LH/FSH ratio (n = 275, MD -0.99, CI -1.44; -0.54) resulted significantly reduced overtime (Fig. 7). Sensitivity analysis using the "leave-one-out" principle did not significantly change the result for the reported outcomes (not shown). Regarding clinical parameters, the KD associated with a significant reduction in BMI (n = 327, MD -4.24, CI -4.88; -3.61) (Supplementary Fig. 1), WC (n = 187, MD -8.42, CI -10.72; -6.11) (Supplementary Fig. 2), WHR (n = 171, MD -0.02, CI -0.03; -0.01) (Supplementary Fig. 3), and fat mass (n = 170, MD -7.74, CI -9.54; -5.95) (Supplementary Fig. 4), independently of study design. A significant reduction in fasting glucose (n = 260, MD -7.80, CI -11.39; -4.21) (Supplementary Fig. 5), fasting insulin (n = 197, MD -9.11, CI -14.79; -3.43) (Supplementary Fig. 6), HOMA-IR (n = 264, MD -2.49, CI -3.71;-1.27) (Supplementary Fig. 7), total cholesterol (n = 229, MD -15.95, CI -31.04; -0.86) (Supplementary Fig. 8), and triglycerides levels (n = 229, MD -44.29, CI -57.31; -31.27) (Supplementary Fig. 9) was also observed to be associated to KD. With KD we observed also a marginally significant increase HDL cholesterol (n = 229, MD 4.53, CI 0.24; 8.81) (Supplementary Fig. 10), and a non-significant decrease in LDL cholesterol (n = 229, MD -8.47, CI -24.30; 7.36) (Supplementary Fig. 11).

When meta-analyzing the data according to the study design, we confirmed all the observed associations in RCTs, with the exception of the increase in HDL level (Supplementary Fig. 10). We also found that, in prospective studies, the reduction in fasting insulin and total cholesterol were no more significant (Supplementary Fig. 6 and 8). The latter, along with HOMA-IR, resulted no more significantly reduced in retrospective studies (Supplementary Fig. 7 and 8). Among secondary outcomes, sensitivity analysis using the "leave-one-out" principle did not significantly changed the findings with the exception of the meta-analyses of total, HDL and LDL Cholesterol (not shown).

Due to significant heterogeneity in the assessment criteria for reproductive outcomes, a quantitative analysis could not be performed. In the study by Cincione and colleagues, out of 17 patients, 5 experienced a natural resumption of their menstrual cycle after years of amenorrhea, and 12 achieved spontaneous pregnancies following numerous unsuccessful attempts []. In the study by Li J and colleagues, the duration of the menstrual cycle was significantly reduced at follow-up compared to baseline in both groups, with no statistically significant difference observed between patients on the KD (32.5 ± 2.67 days vs. 72.50 ± 33.17 days) and controls (33.0 ± 33.17 days vs. 63.00 ± 19.75 days) [].

In the study by Magagnini et al., serum progesterone levels measured on the 21st day increased after VLCKD, with 100% of patients achieving values indicative of ovulation (> 15.9 ng/ml, as reported by the authors) at follow-up []. The study by Mavropoulos and colleagues reported that 2 out of 5 women who completed the dietary protocol achieved pregnancy despite a previous diagnosis of infertility []. Meneghini and colleagues evaluated menstrual cycle regularity and found that it was achieved in 95% of patients undergoing the KD, compared with 60% of cases of those following a Mediterranean protocol []. Lastly, in the work of Pandurevic and colleagues, a significant increase in ovulation (+ 46.1%) was observed after VLCKD, compared to a 21.4% increase following a Mediterranean diet [].

The only primary outcome reported in at least 3 RCTs including a control group was TT. In three of the 4 trials, the control group consisted of patients following an hypocaloric Mediterranean diet protocol [, , ]. In one study, the control group received a pharmacological intervention (Phosphatidylcholine combined with a hormonal contraceptive) []. The KD showed a moderate, statistically significant benefit on TT levels compared to the control intervention, with a high heterogeneity (n = 115 vs. 117, SMD -0.284, CI -0.543, -0.035; p = 0.031) (Fig. 8).Fig. 8Standardized mean differences with 95% Confidence Interval (CI) in total testosterone levels in patients with polycystic ovary syndrome undergoing a ketogenic diet protocol or another type of intervention. sections.title: Discussion
sections.text:
Our key findings suggest that, in PCOS women with obesity or overweight, a KD significantly reduces TT levels, whereas the reduction in FT was not statistically significant. Notably, our results differ partly from those of Khalid et al. []; by not including the RCT by Pandurevic et al. [], they reported a significant reduction in FT levels but did not explore the change in TT. Moreover, by including a larger number of trials and utilizing meta-regression, our study demonstrates that the reduction in TT occurs independently of KD-mediated improvements in metabolic parameters (change in BMI and insulin levels) and/or in the hypothalamic-pituitary axis (reduction in the LH/FSH ratio). This novel finding suggests a direct role of nutritional ketosis on ovarian physiology and steroidogenesis, which might specifically mediate the observed decrease in T levels by KD. While these results are promising, they should be interpreted with caution given the heterogeneity and limited quality of the primary studies included.

PCOS is a highly prevalent endocrine condition affecting women of reproductive age. While its pathogenesis is complex and multifactorial, it’s widely acknowledged that overweight and obesity play a significant role, at least in certain phenotypes of the syndrome []. It has been previously demonstrated that a body weight reduction of approximately 10% can be sufficient to restore ovulation regularity, thereby improving fertility and other syndrome-related symptoms []. Therefore, the aim of the present work was to evaluate all available evidence supporting the role of the KD in PCOS, with a particular focus on ovarian function.

Among the meta-analyzable variables, TT emerged as significantly and independently reduced by KD in the meta-analysis of all included studies. This finding was further strengthened in the meta-analysis of TT, which included 4 RCTs with control arms. Here, the KD proved superior in reducing TT levels compared to other types of interventions (hypocaloric Mediterranean diet or the use of a COC). It’s important to note that the non-significant reduction in FT was also contributed to by an increase in SHBG. In PCOS, SHBG level measurement is also garnering renewed clinical interest due to the fact that a level below 33.4 nmol/l was identified to predict a pathological Liver Fat Score []. Therefore, an increase in SHBG by KD might also improve Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Accordingly, weight loss and improved insulin sensitivity, both common outcomes of a KD, are known to improve hepatic dysfunction [].

In recent years, several studies have been suggesting that KD protocols—differing in duration, composition and calories intake—have beneficial effects on hormonal parameters in women of reproductive age with PCOS and concomitant obesity/overweight. Indeed, changes in hormonal levels appear stronger than those obtained with other protocols, and independent of weight loss. In particular, as noted by Cincione et al., the benefits of KD extend beyond anthropometric measurements and metabolic indices (such as BMI, glucose, insulin, and HOMA-IR) to include FT, LH, FSH and the LH/FSH ratio []. In their study, the advantages of the KD were more pronounced compared to those following a Mediterranean diet, and these differences remained significant even after adjusting for variations in absolute BMI []. Similar results were obtained by Pandurevic et al., in which a VLCKD protocol conducted with the Pronokal® method was compared with Mediterranean LCD []. These findings possibly identify a specific role for nutritional ketosis, which may act on the pathogenetic mechanisms of PCOS, reducing insulin and IGF-1 levels and thus blocking their stimulating effect on ovarian and adrenal androgen production.

KD was also associated with a significant reduction in the LH/FSH ratio. As previously mentioned, In the pathogenesis of PCOS, there is also a change in the hypothalamic secretion pattern of GnRH, due to various mechanisms, including the alteration of negative feedback related to ovarian estrogens and insulin-induced stimulation []. The increase in GnRH pulses leads to an overproduction of LH compared to FSH, resulting in a reversal of their ratio. Although it does not fall among the diagnostic criteria, women with PCOS often exhibit a reversed LH/FSH ratio, two or three times higher than in healthy women, which is generally between 1 and 2. This alteration is responsible for the failure of follicular maturation, anovulation, and LH-induced hyperstimulation of the theca cells, resulting in hyperandrogenism [, ]. From the results of our meta-analysis, it emerged that, both considering all studies and only RCTs, the KD protocol is associated with a statistically significant reduction in LH, accompanied by a reduction in the LH/FSH ratio. Potential mechanisms responsible for KD-associated improvement of LH/FSH ration could be the improvement in insulin sensitivity or the reduced AMH level. In fact, previous researches showed a positive correlation between IR and LH levels or the LH/FSH ratio [] with AMH serving as an mediating factor [].

The study of the effect of the KD on reproductive outcomes has been more complex and has produced non-meta-analyzable results, due to the selection of heterogeneous and poorly comparable outcomes of the studies (Table 5). In addition, the presence of numerous confounding factors, including, foremost, the reproductive condition of the partner, were not taken into account in the considered studies. For all these reasons, we decided to present a qualitative synthesis of the results on reproductive outcomes. Overall, the KD was associated with a positive effect on fertility outcomes investigated in all studies.

Despite the inherent limitations of a meta-analysis, we employed meta-regression to investigate the potential mediating factors behind the KD’s positive effect on hyperandrogenism. It was particularly interesting to observe that the effect on TT appeared to be independent not only of protocol duration and metabolic changes (specifically, reductions in BMI and insulin levels), but also of the reduction in the LH/FSH ratio. This finding aligns with emerging experimental evidence suggesting a direct effect of ketone bodies on ovarian function. For instance, a recent placebo-controlled RCT by Rittig et al. demonstrated that ketone supplementation, namely β-hydroxybutyrate, acutely lowers circulating androgen and glucose levels in women with PCOS, providing compelling support for a mechanism that operates beyond systemic metabolic improvements []. Whether the effect of ketosis is on androgen synthesis, metabolic, or clearance, this has yet to be elucidated.

Further bolstering this hypothesis, animal studies have also highlighted direct ovarian effects of ketosis. For example, research has shown that a KD alleviates the apoptosis of granulosa cells by inhibiting the activation of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway in PCOS []. In addition, β-hydroxybutyrate was demonstrated to suppress activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in response to urate crystals and lipotoxic fatty acids in mice []. Similarly, studies exploring the role of short-chain fatty acids, such as butyric acid, have indicated an improvement in ovarian function and a decreased the expression of local inflammatory factors in the ovary of obese PCOS mice []. These experimental findings collectively suggest that ketone bodies, or the metabolic state of ketosis – especially in VLEKT -, may exert a direct influence on ovarian steroidogenesis and overall ovarian health, independently of the classic pathways involving weight loss or hypothalamic-pituitary regulation. Regarding human studies, in women with obesity undergoing a VLEKT protocol, multiple regression analysis identified the reduction in High-sensitivity C-reactive protein as the main predictor of MASLD improvement, explaining almost 66% of the variance []. Ultimately, this anti-inflammatory action may complement the reduction in hyperinsulinemia to restore ovarian function and improve the biochemical profile of women with PCOS.

Our meta-analysis has several limitations. Firstly, the limited number of analyzed studies, mostly of low quality, with small sample sizes, short durations, and only a minority represented by RCTs. Regarding the considered outcomes, there is often a lack of uniformity in the methods of biochemical parameter measurement. This is particularly important for determining T concentrations, where the gold standard method is LC/MS, which is limited by its availability and high costs. In several included studies, FT was obtained by direct radioimmunological or ELISA assays. These methods often exhibit limited accuracy and poor precision and sensitivity, thus reducing the strength of the results. Concerning the variables considered in various studies, the role of physical activity has not been evaluated in patients undergoing KD, even though it constitutes a first-line therapy in PCOS management.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.text: In conclusion, while our meta-analysis indicates a reduced biochemical hyperandrogenism—particularly a reduction in TT—and a reduction in the LH/FSH ratio among women with PCOS following a KD, the evidence remains preliminary. Our findings also suggest a specific effect of ketosis on ovarian function acting alongside metabolic improvements, but a direct causal link cannot be definitively established. Owing to the low quality and heterogeneous nature of the available studies, including both RCTs and observational data, our conclusions must be viewed as hypothesis-generating. Larger, high-quality RCTs are essential to consolidate this evidence and determine clinical efficacy.
